name: Digital Channels
description: Design, operation, and continuous improvement of the bank's customer-facing digital touchpoints and the underlying integration layer that connects them to core systems and third parties. The capability spans the authenticated online banking portal, mobile banking application, the Open Banking API programme (including PSD2/OBIE compliance and commercial TPP connectivity), and customer communications orchestration. It is the primary channel through which retail and SME customers interact with the bank in daily life and the primary source of data about customer behaviour that informs product and service design.
mandate_source: Payment Services Regulations 2017 (PSR 2017) implementing PSD2 — mandates access to payment accounts for TPPs (AISPs and PISPs)
Open Banking Implementation Entity (OBIE) / Open Banking Ltd standards — technical standards for Open Banking APIs
FCA Electronic Money and Payment Institutions (EMPI) supervisory framework
FCA Consumer Duty (PS22/9) — digital channel design must meet the Understanding outcome; consumer support must be accessible
Equality Act 2010 and WCAG 2.1 AA — digital accessibility obligations for all customer-facing channels
UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018 — customer data handling in digital channels
FCA Operational Resilience Policy Statement (PS21/3) — important business services including digital banking must meet impact tolerances
PRA/FCA Outsourcing and Third Party Risk Management (SS2/21) — digital platform vendors as critical third parties

table_stakes: Mobile banking application with biometric authentication, account balance, and transaction history — Monzo and Starling have made real-time push notifications and instant transaction display the minimum viable standard
Online banking portal (web) for bill payment, CHAPS/BACS, standing orders, and direct debit management
In-app card controls: freeze/unfreeze, spend limits, merchant blocking — pioneered by Monzo, now expected by all UK retail customers
Secure message centre and in-app customer support
Open Banking-compliant Account Information Service (AISP) and Payment Initiation Service (PISP) APIs meeting OBIE standards
Two-factor and Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) compliant with PSD2 RTS
Digital onboarding for new accounts (eKYC, identity verification)
differentiators: Proactive financial insights derived from transaction categorisation — Monzo Trends and Starling Spending Insights set the benchmark; banks with richer data (mortgages, business banking, wealth) can provide genuinely more complete picture
Seamless cross-product visibility: current account, savings, mortgage, credit card, and investment balance in a single authenticated view — neobanks lack the product depth to offer this

SME and commercial banking features in a unified app: invoice management, payroll integration, multi-user permissions, and spend analytics — Tide and Starling Business have set strong benchmarks but lack the commercial bank's credit and trade finance depth
Embedded personal finance management (PFM) with account aggregation across multiple banks using Open Banking data
Variable Recurring Payments (VRP) for sweeping and intelligent payment automation once JROC implementation matures
Hyper-personalised communications triggered by life events and behavioural signals
disruptors: Monzo (8m+ UK accounts): sets the UX benchmark for mobile banking; real-time notifications, spending analytics, and instant customer support have raised customer expectations permanently; Monzo Plus/Max subscription model demonstrates willingness to pay for premium digital features
Starling Bank (4m+ accounts): strong in SME/business banking; Marketplace model shows the potential for open banking-based product aggregation within a banking app; acquired by Nationwide 2025

Revolut (10m+ UK users): super-app ambitions — banking, investment, travel insurance, crypto, and salary advance in a single app; UK banking licence secured 2024; most direct threat to incumbent multi-product bundle

Chase UK (JP Morgan): launched 2021 with 1% cashback and a polished mobile UX backed by JP Morgan's technology investment; targeting Monzo's premium mass-market segment with product depth incumbents can match
Wise: dominant in international payments and FX; has expanded into multi-currency accounts; a threat to the bank's FX revenue on international transactions

Open banking middleware providers (TrueLayer, Yapily, Bud): enable fintechs to build bank-quality account aggregation and payment initiation without a banking licence — lowering the barrier to entry for challengers
unbundling: Account aggregation unbundled by Open Banking: PFM apps (Emma, Cleo, Money Dashboard) aggregate balances across banks using AISP APIs — the bank's own data no longer has to sit in the bank's own app

Payment initiation unbundled: PISPs (Volt, Modulr, TrueLayer Pay) enable merchants and fintechs to initiate payments from customer bank accounts without going through card networks, compressing interchange revenue

Customer communications unbundled: specialist platforms (Twilio, MessageBird/CM.com, customer.io, Braze) have replaced in-house SMS/email/push notification infrastructure — banks buy communications-as-a-service rather than building notification engines
Identity and KYC unbundled: digital identity providers (Yoti, Onfido/Entrust, Jumio) handle document verification, liveness checks, and identity binding — banks integrate rather than build

Branch network declining sharply: UK branch count fell from ~9,000 in 2015 to under 4,000 by 2024; digital self-service replacing the branch for routine transactions, with call centre and digital chat as the residual support model
Call centre interactions: cost per call centre interaction £4–8 vs £0.10–0.30 per digital interaction — economic pressure accelerating digital self-service substitution
rebundling: Revolut re-bundling payments, FX, investment, insurance, and salary advance — the most aggressive super-app play in the UK market
Monzo Premium/Max re-bundling banking with travel insurance, credit monitoring, and cashback — premium subscription model creating a bundled value proposition

Open Banking-enabled account aggregation within the bank's own app (buy-side rebundling): banks integrating third-party account data to become the 'financial hub' rather than ceding the aggregation layer to fintechs
switching_drivers: Mobile UX quality: Monzo's UX benchmarks (real-time notifications, instant freeze, transparent spending breakdown) are now the table stakes — legacy mobile apps with 3-5 day transaction delays are a primary switching driver

Current Account Switch Service (CASS) friction reduction: 7-day switching guarantee has lowered switching cost; combined with strong neobank incentives (cashback, interest, features) drives current account churn
Digital feature gaps: absence of in-app mortgage management, investment dashboard, or PFM creates switching pressure among digitally-engaged customers
Customer support quality: digital-first customers expect in-app chat resolution within minutes; failure to deliver drives defection to Monzo/Starling
Open Banking portability: customers can now see all their accounts in one place via AISPs — reduces lock-in and makes product comparison easier

current: PSD2 (Payment Services Regulations 2017): mandates Open Banking access; requires banks to provide APIs for AISPs and PISPs; 90-day re-authentication, SCA exemptions, and fallback interface requirements currently enforced
OBIE / Open Banking Ltd standards: Version 3.1.x API standards govern the technical implementation of Open Banking; Open Banking Ltd (successor to OBIE) continues standard development post-CMA Order
SCA / RTS on SCA: Strong Customer Authentication requirements under PSD2 RTS; applies to online payments and account access; UK FCA has implemented with OBIE-specific adaptations

FCA Consumer Duty — Understanding and Support outcomes: digital channel design must ensure customers can understand products and get support when needed; applies to app UX, notification design, and customer service routing
WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility: Equality Act 2010 digital accessibility obligations; FCA increasingly treating inaccessible digital channels as a Consumer Duty breach
FCA Operational Resilience (PS21/3): mobile banking and online banking identified as important business services; impact tolerance framework requires defined maximum tolerable downtime
incoming_2_3_years: PSD3 / PSR (European Commission proposal 2023 — UK will diverge but influence HM Treasury): expanded scope for Open Banking; strengthened PISP rights; potential for data sharing beyond payment accounts; UK HM Treasury's National Payments Vision (2024) signals alignment with VRP expansion and smart data schemes

Variable Recurring Payments (VRP) commercial expansion: JROC (Joint Regulatory Oversight Committee) roadmap requires banks to enable commercial VRP beyond sweeping use cases by 2026; will require significant API investment and creates new competitive dynamics in subscription and recurring payment markets

UK Digital Identity and Attributes Trust Framework (DIATF): DSIT framework for certified digital identity providers; banks as identity relying parties and potential identity providers; may reshape KYC and onboarding flows materially

Smart Data Schemes: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 creates the legislative basis for Smart Data beyond banking (energy, telecoms, pensions); banking must be prepared to extend Open Banking data sharing model to new sectors

FCA / PSR APP Fraud reimbursement (mandatory from October 2023, PSR PS23/3): Authorised Push Payment fraud reimbursement obligations — digital channel design must incorporate real-time fraud warnings, confirmation of payee (CoP), and friction-based payment intervention
enforcement_signals: FCA Consumer Duty supervisory work on digital channel design (2024): FCA reviewing whether digital journeys meet the Understanding outcome — specific focus on notification clarity, overdraft and fee disclosures in app, and customer support accessibility
PSR APP fraud enforcement: PSR has named specific banks in league tables for APP fraud vulnerability; banks with weak payment friction controls face both reputational and regulatory risk

FCA / CMA Open Banking monitoring: CMA remains the primary enforcer of Open Banking obligations for the nine largest banks; ongoing monitoring of API performance, availability, and incident reporting — OBIE published performance dashboards publicly

FCA Operational Resilience enforcement: post-PS21/3, FCA has indicated it will test firms' operational resilience through stress testing and incident-based reviews; digital channel outages above impact tolerances are reportable events
ICO enforcement on cookie compliance and consent management in digital channels: PECR and UK GDPR enforcement against banks for non-compliant web/app tracking practices

platform_options: Backbase: digital banking platform covering mobile banking, online banking, and SME banking; modular architecture allowing incremental adoption; used by NatWest, ABN AMRO, and several tier-2 UK banks; strong in engagement banking layer over core systems
Temenos Infinity: digital banking front-end platform; pre-integrated with Temenos Transact core; used by smaller UK challenger banks; less dominant in tier-1 context
Salesforce Financial Services Cloud: CRM and customer communications orchestration; used by some UK banks for relationship management and communications layer

TrueLayer: Open Banking middleware and payment initiation; used by over 200 fintechs and banks for AISP/PISP connectivity; strong UK regulatory track record; also offers PayDirect (instant bank payments)
Yapily: Open Banking connectivity platform covering 2,000+ institutions across Europe; API aggregation layer for multi-bank data and payment initiation
Bud Financial: AI-powered transaction categorisation, Open Banking data enrichment, and PFM insights engine; used by HSBC and Standard Chartered
Twilio: cloud communications platform covering SMS, push notifications, email, voice, and WhatsApp; programmable API model; dominant in developer-led communications infrastructure
MessageBird / CM.com: enterprise communications platform with stronger compliance tooling than Twilio for regulated industries
customer.io / Braze: customer engagement and lifecycle marketing platforms; event-triggered communications orchestration; used by digital-native banks for onboarding, nudge, and retention campaigns
Onfido / Entrust / Jumio: digital identity verification for onboarding and re-authentication; integrated with UK DIATF certified identity schemes
Mulesoft / Apigee (Google): API management and integration platform for internal and external API programme governance
must_build_in_house: Core mobile and online banking application (at least the authenticated product experience layer): the bank's app is the primary brand touchpoint and competitive differentiation vehicle — outsourcing the entire front-end to a white-label platform risks commoditising the customer experience

Open Banking API programme ownership and governance: the bank must own the API product roadmap, TPP onboarding policy, consent management, and incident management — these are CMA/PSR regulated obligations that cannot be delegated

Fraud and transaction monitoring logic: real-time payment intervention, APP fraud warning triggers, and confirmation of payee (CoP) integration must be owned in-house for PSR compliance and liability management
Customer data model and consent management: UK GDPR consent, preferences, and communication opt-in/out must be bank-controlled for regulatory accountability
Operational resilience framework for digital channels: impact tolerance definitions, recovery time objectives, and incident reporting to FCA/PRA must be owned by the bank
buy_candidates: Open Banking connectivity middleware: TrueLayer or Yapily for TPP connectivity, token management, and multi-institution data aggregation — building proprietary AISP/PISP connectivity to 50+ banks is not efficient; specialist providers maintain it as core IP

Customer communications delivery infrastructure: Twilio or MessageBird for SMS, push, and email delivery — the delivery layer is commodity; the bank's value is in the orchestration logic and personalisation on top

Transaction categorisation and enrichment: Bud or similar for ML-powered transaction labelling — high build cost for training data and model maintenance; specialist providers have network effects from multi-bank data

Digital identity verification: Onfido or Jumio for document verification and liveness — regulatory standards change frequently; specialist providers maintain compliance with DIATF and FCA eKYC expectations
API management gateway: Apigee or AWS API Gateway for internal and external API programme governance — commodity infrastructure with strong managed service options

primary_revenue_streams: Digital channel is primarily a cost centre and retention vehicle — its revenue contribution is indirect through reduced churn, increased product cross-sell, and lower cost-to-serve vs branch and call centre
Open Banking APIs: commercial VRP fees (emerging, post-JROC Phase 2); potential API monetisation for TPP premium access tiers

Digital sales conversion: mortgage applications, savings account openings, credit card applications, and investment onboarding completed in-app generate product revenue attributed to the digital channel
FX on international payments executed through the app — margin on cross-currency transactions initiated digitally
Premium subscription digital features: following Monzo Plus/Max model, potential for a fee-bearing premium tier (travel insurance, cashback, enhanced PFM) bundled with the digital channel
margin_pressure: Cost of digital channel maintenance and continuous improvement: mobile OS updates (iOS/Android), security patching, WCAG compliance, and feature parity with neobanks create a permanent investment treadmill
API programme compliance cost: OBIE/Open Banking Ltd standards updates, incident monitoring, and CMA reporting add ongoing operational cost without direct revenue

Fraud reimbursement under PSR APP rules: mandatory reimbursement for authorised push payment fraud up to £85,000 creates a direct P&L impact — digital channel design must reduce fraud incidence to protect margin
Open Banking payment initiation cannibilising card interchange: PISP-initiated payments bypass card networks, reducing interchange revenue on transactions migrating from card to account-to-account

Customer support cost for digital channel failures: when digital channels are unavailable or unintuitive, customers escalate to call centre — each call centre interaction costs 20–40x more than digital self-service
cross_sell_hooks: In-app product recommendations triggered by transaction data: mortgage affordability nudges for renters, savings prompts for current account balance patterns, investment onboarding for customers receiving salary into account

Open Banking account aggregation as PFM hub: customers who aggregate external accounts within the bank's app have higher engagement and cross-sell conversion rates (industry data: 2–3x higher product holding)
Business banking cross-sell for SME digital users: sole traders and small businesses using the personal app are prospects for business accounts, invoice finance, and merchant services
Wealth management referral from digital PFM: cashflow insights revealing savings surplus or investment capacity trigger warm referrals to the wealth management capability (CAP-006)

sub_capabilities.name: Online Banking
sub_capabilities.description: Browser-based authenticated banking portal providing account management, payments (CHAPS, BACS, Faster Payments, international), direct debit and standing order management, statements, and secure messaging. The primary channel for desktop-based transactional banking and for customers who require accessibility features best delivered via web.

promotion_test.market_evidence: Online Banking shares the same authenticated session model, the same customer data layer, the same payments infrastructure, and the same fraud monitoring as Mobile Banking. Market evidence shows these are converging rather than diverging: Monzo and Starling launched as mobile-only and added web banking as a secondary channel under the same product team. NatWest, Lloyds, and Barclays all manage online and mobile banking as a single Digital Channels product line. The technology stack (API-first, single customer identity layer, shared notification engine) makes a deployment boundary between online and mobile artificial and costly. WCAG accessibility obligations apply equally to both channels. The online portal's distinct characteristic is the browser interface and accessibility-first design, not a different business capability. Criteria met: 0 of 4. RETAIN.

sub_capabilities.name: Mobile Banking
sub_capabilities.description: Native iOS and Android banking applications providing the full transactional feature set of online banking plus mobile-native features: biometric authentication, real-time push notifications, in-app card controls, spend analytics, and camera-based document capture. The primary interaction channel for the majority of retail customers.

promotion_test.market_evidence: Mobile Banking is the highest-engagement touchpoint in the Digital Channels capability but does not warrant promotion to a standalone capability. Monzo, Starling, and Chase UK demonstrate that mobile-first is the channel strategy, not a separate business domain — their entire proposition is delivered through a single mobile app without an independent product capability boundary. The technology and regulatory obligations (SCA, PSD2, fraud, data protection) are shared with Online Banking and are managed by a single Digital Channels team. The development lifecycle (iOS/Android release cadence, app store submission, WCAG compliance) does not constitute a distinct business lifecycle — it is a delivery cycle within the same capability. Demand scaling (active user growth) is correlated with product growth, not independent of it. Criteria met: 0 of 4. RETAIN.

sub_capabilities.name: Open Banking APIs
sub_capabilities.description: The bank's regulated Open Banking programme: OBIE/Open Banking Ltd-compliant APIs for Account Information Services (AISP) and Payment Initiation Services (PISP); TPP onboarding and consent management; the emerging Variable Recurring Payments (VRP) capability; commercial API products for fintech partners; and the governance, monitoring, and incident management required by CMA Order and PSR obligations.

promotion_test.market_evidence: Open Banking APIs meets all four promotion criteria, making it a strong promotion candidate on the test. However, it is RETAINED within Digital Channels at this stage for the following reasons grounded in market and organisational evidence. (1) Distinct participants: true — TPPs (TrueLayer, Yapily, Monzo, Revolut, hundreds of fintechs) are participants absent from Online/Mobile Banking; FCA-registered AISPs and PISPs are subject to separate regulatory oversight. (2) Separate regulatory framework: true — PSD2/PSR 2017, CMA Open Banking Order, OBIE standards, and the emerging JROC framework for VRP are distinct from the general digital channel regulatory environment. (3) Distinct lifecycle: true — API versioning (OBIE v3.1.x), TPP onboarding, consent lifecycle management, and the commercial VRP product roadmap operate on a cycle independent of the consumer mobile app. (4) Independent scalability: true — API call volume scales with TPP ecosystem growth (millions of API calls per day from aggregators like TrueLayer) independently of the bank's own customer base growth. RETAIN rationale: Despite meeting 4/4 criteria, Open Banking APIs is retained within Digital Channels because (a) the API surface is currently tightly coupled to the same core banking integration layer shared with Online/Mobile Banking — a promotion would require a clean API gateway boundary that does not yet exist in the target architecture; (b) the commercial VRP and premium API product opportunity is nascent (JROC Phase 2 timeline extends to 2026) — promoting to a standalone capability before the commercial model is validated risks over-engineering the boundary; (c) the bank's CMA Order obligations assign accountability to a single senior manager across the full Open Banking programme, which currently includes the digital channel — splitting the accountability at this stage creates regulatory risk. Recommendation: schedule a capability promotion review for Open Banking APIs at the point when the commercial VRP product launches and the API gateway has been established as a clean architectural boundary — likely 2026. At that point, the business case for a standalone CAP-00X (Open Banking & Embedded Finance) is strong.

sub_capabilities.name: Customer Communications
sub_capabilities.description: Orchestration, delivery, and governance of all bank-initiated customer communications across digital channels: push notifications, SMS, in-app messages, email, and WhatsApp Business. Includes event-triggered transactional notifications (payment confirmations, fraud alerts, balance nudges), marketing communications (subject to consent), and regulated communications (statement availability, fee notices). Operates over third-party delivery infrastructure (Twilio, MessageBird) with the bank owning the orchestration logic, consent management, and compliance controls.

promotion_test.market_evidence: Customer Communications is a capability area where market unbundling is pronounced — Twilio, MessageBird/CM.com, Braze, and customer.io have made communications delivery a utility, and banks universally buy delivery infrastructure rather than building it. However, unbundling the delivery layer does not constitute a separate business capability at the bank level. The communications orchestration logic (what trigger, what message, what channel, what consent state) is inseparable from the digital channel product experience: a payment confirmation push notification is part of the Mobile Banking sub-capability's contract with the customer; a fraud alert is part of the fraud monitoring control. Monzo's highly-regarded notification experience is not managed as a separate capability — it is owned by the same product team as the mobile app. The distinct participants criterion fails because the bank's customers are the same participants receiving all digital communications. The regulatory framework (UK GDPR consent, PECR, FCA Consumer Duty communications outcome) applies to all digital channel touchpoints equally. The lifecycle criterion fails because communications campaigns and transactional notifications are driven by product lifecycle events, not an independent delivery schedule. Twilio and Braze as buy candidates sit within the Customer Communications sub-capability as infrastructure — their independent existence as platforms does not create a separate bank capability. Criteria met: 0 of 4. RETAIN.

design_decisions.decision: Retain Open Banking APIs within Digital Channels despite meeting 4/4 promotion criteria, with a scheduled promotion review in 2026 when VRP commercial phase and API gateway architecture are established.
design_decisions.rationale: The promotion test is necessary but not sufficient for promotion — the deployment boundary must also be clean and the commercial model must be validated. The current state is that the Open Banking API surface is coupled to the same core banking integration layer as Online/Mobile Banking. Promoting now would require simultaneously creating an architectural boundary that does not exist, which front-loads delivery risk. The right sequencing is: (1) establish API gateway as a clean boundary in the technical architecture; (2) launch commercial VRP product and validate the revenue model; (3) promote to standalone capability. The promotion criteria score provides a documented basis for the future promotion decision without forcing it prematurely.
alternatives_considered: Promote Open Banking APIs to a standalone capability immediately (CAP-00X: Open Banking and Embedded Finance)
Create a separate Open Finance capability encompassing Open Banking APIs, data sharing, and embedded finance partnerships
design_decisions.rejected_because: Immediate promotion would create a deployment boundary without a corresponding architectural boundary, introducing integration seams at exactly the point where the bank faces CMA-mandated API availability obligations. An outage at that boundary would be a regulatory incident. The broader Open Finance scope is premature — Smart Data schemes are in early legislative phase (Data Use and Access Act 2025) and the commercial model for data monetisation is not yet validated.

design_decisions.decision: Classify Customer Communications as RETAIN within Digital Channels rather than creating a standalone Marketing Technology or Customer Engagement capability.
design_decisions.rationale: The distinction between transactional communications (payment confirmation, fraud alert) and marketing communications (product offer) is real but does not constitute a capability boundary at this stage. Both are governed by the same consent management framework (UK GDPR, PECR), both use the same delivery infrastructure (Twilio/MessageBird), and both are triggered by events originating in the digital channel. Creating a separate capability would require duplicating the consent management and data layer, and would create ambiguity about ownership of real-time transactional notifications which are integral to the mobile banking contract with the customer.
alternatives_considered: Create a standalone Customer Engagement or MarTech capability to own lifecycle marketing, push campaigns, and customer.io/Braze orchestration
Place Customer Communications under a separate CRM/Marketing capability rather than Digital Channels
design_decisions.rejected_because: A standalone MarTech capability is appropriate if the bank is running sophisticated multi-channel lifecycle marketing at scale with a dedicated team and separate P&L — that is a future state, not the current operating model. The transactional notification use case (fraud alerts, payment confirmations, balance nudges) is too tightly coupled to the mobile banking product experience to sit in a separate capability without creating significant coordination overhead.

design_decisions.decision: Treat branch and call centre as out of scope for CAP-007, scoping Digital Channels to digital-only touchpoints (web, mobile, API, digital communications).
design_decisions.rationale: Branch and call centre represent a distinct operating model, workforce type, property footprint, and declining investment trajectory. Including them in Digital Channels would create a capability with incompatible lifecycles: digital channels are on a high-velocity improvement cycle; branch network is on a rationalisation/closure programme. Separating them allows each to be managed against its own investment case and performance metrics.
alternatives_considered: Create a broad 'Customer Channels' capability encompassing branch, call centre, and digital under a unified omnichannel framework
Include branch digital enablement (in-branch tablets, self-service kiosks) within CAP-007
design_decisions.rejected_because: An omnichannel 'Customer Channels' capability at this scope would be too large to be a coherent deployment unit. Branch digital enablement (kiosks, tablets) is a branch investment decision, not a digital channel product decision — including it conflates the physical and digital investment cycles. The industry direction (declining branch count, digital substitution) makes the separation increasingly clean over the planning horizon.

deployment_notes: Digital Channels is NOT a capability in the architectural sense. It is a channel layer sitting outside the system boundary. Online Banking, Mobile Banking, and Customer Communications are channel services that call capability REST APIs synchronously. Open Banking APIs (CAP-007.03) remains a distinct capability if promoted.
